stories.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia return shows the U.S.-China AI race is about more than chips
stories.summary: Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO demonstrates that the U.S.-China artificial intelligence race is not just about semiconductors, but tech talent too.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia return shows the U.S.-China AI race is about more than chips
sources.text: BEIJING — Jensen Huang ' s return to Nvidia as its CEO underscores how the U.S.-China artificial intelligence race is not only about semiconductors, but tech talent. "We have to protect our geniuses, and he's clearly a genius," Donald Trump told CNBC about his intervention to bring Huang back. If not, Trump warned, the founder of the AI chip giant could hypothetically have taken a job in China. The concern reflects how Chinese AI companies have been narrowing the gap with their U.S. counterparts, not just in models, but now in engineering and research talent. China has surpassed the U.S. by share of global AI talent in just three years, according to Carnegie Endowment research. Nvidia "was shaken without a single chip or model changing," said Winston Ma, an AI investor and adjunct professor of law at New York University. "Whoever builds and keeps that human layer will hold the rest of the stack." Huang resigned Nov. 12 after reports of an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes has links to Chinese intelligence. He returned on Nov. 23, news which sent Nvidia shares surging. More than 30 years ago, Huang founded Nvidia as a gaming graphics chip company. The semiconductors gradually became used to mine cryptocurrencies, and now, training cutting-edge AI models. Huang has more advanced tech coming, Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers on Monday. "He's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me, that nobody else understands," Trump said. "Jensen could take the next plane to China, and I guarantee you, they would give him whatever he wanted, and then and then they automatically have, you know, all of the things," Trump said. He acknowledged there was "never even a suggestion" that the Nvidia founder was recruited by China. Trump returned to the U.S. over the weekend from Shenzhen, China, where he met Chinese President Xi Jinping. Earlier in the month, turmoil around Huang's future at Nvidia had gripped global attention. For Huang's supporters, talent was a critical part of the argument, said Damien Ma, director and Maurice R. Greenberg Director's Chair of Carnegie China. As the incident has increased scrutiny on the people involved in the U.S.-China tech race, Ma said he's closely watching whether either country restricts AI engineers from leaving. While he expects limited policy changes, other countries such as Singapore and South Korea could benefit from an inflow of AI talent, he added. Already, many companies are using a mixed-market approach, given engineers in the U.S. make two or three times as much as their Chinese counterparts due in part to foreign exchange rates and AI company valuations. In the U.S., "you need to have a lot of money to recruit them," said Alex Lu, founder of LSY Consulting — and that can get expensive. Lu cited the founder of a U.S. consumer research firm, who opted to hire engineers based in China after visiting the country. It's an anecdote that's frequently repeated by analysts, sometimes with U.S.-trained Chinese staff based in Singapore. Chinese companies are "very, very aggressive in getting good talent from the U.S. ," said Tidalwave Solutions Partner Rachel Wu, who recruits for large Chinese tech companies and startups. She also said a Meta engineer in Canada took an offer from a Chinese AI startup for a salary of 1.4 million yuan ($210,000), in addition to stock options. "There is some truth to Trump's comments given Jensen's knowledge of the AI industry and supply chain," said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst of Omdia. "It would be unwise for the U.S. to let this saga continue to affect its AI ambition, especially when that ambition includes slowing down Chinese progress in AI." However, Rui Ma, founder of advisory Tech Buzz China, said Huang's background of being a founder makes it more likely that he would have started his own company, rather than taking a managerial role at one. She also noted Huang's "deep belief in America" and laws that would block him from using his access to TSMC and other suppliers to help a Chinese company. The U.S. has restricted China's access to advanced Nvidia semiconductors over the last four years. But in early 2025, DeepSeek upended assumptions that chip restrictions could keep Chinese AI capabilities well behind that of the U.S. A few years ago, only the U.S. and Singapore had the kind of AI talent that Chinese companies were looking for, Wu said. "Today we see the gap has been filled," she said, adding the supply of local talent has increased in the last two to three years. "The demand is huge," Wu said, saying one ex- Alibaba AI engineering candidate with seven years of experience had more than five offers. Switching between companies can result in a 25% to 30% pay bump, Wu said. She expects the trend to persist for another two years, although the increase in compensation may not be as high. Still, restricted access to advanced AI chips plays a role in where the best researchers choose to work. It's a question of "where I can do my further research and do I have enough resources to do my research," said Lu. He said industry research suggests "China is becoming a really important pool for talent, while the U.S. is paying 80% of the money."

sources.name: Wired AI
sources.title: Jensen Huang’s Return Shows Nvidia Is Too Big to Police
sources.text: Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO signals that the chipmaker may have grown too important to the stock market for the US government to hold it accountable for national security lapses, intelligence and export-control experts warn WIRED. The move also undercuts the warnings Washington routinely issues to American companies and foreign governments about Beijing’s pursuit of US technology, they say. Nvidia’s board brought back Huang on Monday, 11 days after he resigned amid revelations of extramarital affairs —one of them with Alice Huang, a woman US intelligence suspects has ties to China’s Ministry of State Security. The board said input from “senior levels of the United States government” left it confident that his return poses no national security risk . President Donald Trump told The Wall Street Journal he lobbied the board directly and through intermediaries, and that Nvidia’s falling share price helped his case. The board acted before its own investigation of Huang had concluded, and while the Justice Department is pursuing a criminal probe of Megaspeed—a Singapore company Alice Huang once ran—over the alleged diversion of Nvidia chips to China. Alice Huang is also under investigation , according to director of national intelligence Jay Clayton. The experts tell WIRED they worry more about the precedent Huang’s return sets than about Huang himself. Some say the scrutiny now on him makes further compromise unlikely. But Beijing may already have gained insight into Nvidia’s chip designs and its private conversations with the White House and Congress, or, through Megaspeed, obtained the chips themselves, they say, and no one has publicly established what, if anything, it got. Several want to know who gave the board its assurances and on what basis, and whether the government ran a counterintelligence damage assessment or simply made a political judgment. They also say the administration has repeatedly failed to enforce its own export controls, and that when intelligence concerns appear to yield to market pressure, US warnings about China start to sound negotiable, to Beijing’s benefit. “If intelligence assessments are seen to be overridden, selectively interpreted, or publicly dismissed for political or commercial reasons, this could undermine long-term confidence in the independence of national security institutions,” says Tahlia Peterson, a cyber and technology research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a London defense think tank. “That would be damaging to US national security, and potentially advantageous to Beijing.” Advisers briefed Trump at least twice on Alice Huang’s links to Chinese intelligence before the affair became public, and both times he played down their concerns, The New York Times reported Sunday . When the Journal asked him on Monday about Republican lawmakers who say Huang’s return endangers national security, Trump pointed to Nvidia’s rebounding stock. “Some tech companies have become so big—and so important to the stock market—that Washington is reluctant to hold them accountable for national security lapses,” says Edward Fishman, director of the Council on Foreign Relations’ Maurice R. Greenberg Center for Geoeconomics. Fishman sees a parallel in Wall Street’s slow reckoning with sanctions. “It took years of aggressive enforcement to get banks to take US sanctions compliance seriously,” he says. “We haven’t seen anything comparable in the tech sector, which helps explain why US export controls remain so weak and leaky.” Reinstating Huang on the administration's assurances before Nvidia’s own investigation has concluded “does not inspire confidence that meaningful enforcement is coming,” he says. Emily Kilcrease, a former deputy assistant US trade representative who now directs the Energy, Economics, and Security program at the Center for a New American Security, says the administration’s record gives little reason to take those assurances at face value. “We cannot rely on the administration’s judgment, as it has repeatedly failed to enforce export controls over the past year,” she says. On Monday, the Commerce Department added Megaspeed to its trade blacklist, and the administration has recently moved to tighten rules on China’s AI industry. But Kilcrease says it acted only under pressure. “Given the poor track record on export controls and their broader accommodationist stance toward China, it’s fair to ask whether they are willing to really enforce the new controls,” she says. The board’s assurances appear to have come mostly from the Justice Department. Attorney general Todd Blanche allegedly told Trump and vice president JD Vance on Saturday that Huang was neither a target nor a subject of any department investigation, and that the department had no evidence he had broken the law or posed a national security risk, the Journal reports. Vance then reportedly sought assurances for the board that the administration did not consider Huang a threat and that he would not face criminal charges. Trump told the Times he also consulted Clayton before pushing for Huang’s return. (“I can’t do this and then all of a sudden have somebody get indicted,” he said.) Nvidia did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment. Whether Huang broke any laws is a separate question from whether Beijing gained anything through him. “Did [the assurances] reflect a counterintelligence damage assessment by the intelligence community or the FBI, or were they political in nature?” says Jessica Brandt, a senior fellow for technology and national security at the Council on Foreign Relations who previously directed the Foreign Malign Influence Center at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. “Lawmakers should press on that.” Senior officials may have seen intelligence that isn’t public, so the assurances shouldn’t just be dismissed, says Sunny Cheung, a China studies fellow at the Jamestown Foundation. “However, we still don’t know who pr

sources.name: TechCrunch AI
sources.title: The questions Jensen Huang and Nvidia will still have to answer about Megaspeed
sources.text: Jensen Huang’s return as CEO to Nvidia hasn’t eased the scrutiny the company faces. The chipmaker still needs to address multiple inquiries into allegations that its advanced GPUs were smuggled into China by a customer, the Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed, in violation of U.S. export rules designed to slow China’s development of frontier AI models. The central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where those chips ended up and whether Huang’s affair with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed’s assurances. Huang’s return doesn’t settle that. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche has suggested Nvidia isn’t a target of an investigation, but California’s attorney general and Congress are pressing ahead, and the Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating, too. The U.S. government opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 and requested information from Nvidia about its billions of dollars in sales to the company, concerned that some of the chips Megaspeed bought for data center projects in Malaysia were in fact being diverted to China. Singapore also began investigating similar allegations in 2025. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing. Diversion of this kind would be a fairly routine issue for a company like Nvidia, whose in-demand chips are the targets of smugglers and resellers. When it comes to compliance and liability for export-control violations, Nvidia and other chip sellers need assurances that the end users of their chips are obeying the rules. However, they also cannot ignore other information that might call the reliability of those assurances into question, export-control attorneys told TechCrunch. And that’s why Jensen Huang’s affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang was such a problem for Nvidia, likely even more so than her alleged role as a source for Chinese intelligence agencies. If Nvidia personnel, from lower-level employees up to the CEO, had reason to believe that statements from Megaspeed weren’t reliable, the attorneys said, that would increase the company’s legal risk. “Government investigators likely would want to know, notwithstanding whatever formal assurances were exchanged between the parties, what anyone at Nvidia actually knew about the end use and end users of the chips,” Dan Fisher-Owens, an attorney at the firm Berliner Corcoran & Rowe, told TechCrunch last week. The concern Nvidia’s board faced when it decided to oust Huang is that he knew more about what Megaspeed was doing with Nvidia’s products than was reflected in any of the compliance statements. The Wall Street Journal reported that Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, were part of a network of businesses that funneled chips to a company in Shanghai. Kang also reportedly introduced his wife to Jensen Huang, whom he had known for a decade. On Monday, the U.S. government added Megaspeed and its affiliates to a list of companies restricted from U.S. trade due to national security concerns. The U.S. also issued new rules last week barring large data centers that purchase U.S. chips from serving customers in China and other nations seen as problematic by the U.S. government. Nvidia, meanwhile, said it would stop selling licensed chips to China and laid out plans to hire its first compliance officer and create a new board committee focused on export controls. Nvidia’s board said it reinstated Huang on Monday after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that left it confident his return posed no national security risk. President Donald Trump later said he called into the meeting to give them that assurance. In a news conference Tuesday, Blanche said that Nvidia was “a good corporate citizen” and suggested it is not the target of an investigation, but Blanche declined to answer questions about the government’s investigation into Megaspeed, which the Justice Department said was ongoing as recently as last week. “When you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don’t know what you’re talking about,” Blanche said. Other authorities may be more demanding. Nvidia faces investigations by California Attorney General Rob Bonta and, reportedly , the SEC, both tied to its corporate disclosures. While many details of the investigation still aren’t known, short sellers complained about the company’s decision to stop breaking out its exports to Singapore in financial filings after journalists raised concerns about chip diversion. Members of Congress from both parties say they want answers from Nvidia, with many citing alarm about China and some questioning the White House’s role in Huang’s return. Three committees in the House of Representatives will privately interview Huang and Nvidia’s top lawyer, Tim Teter, next week. Teter reportedly intervened in the Department of Commerce’s investigation of Megaspeed last year. “We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of Nvidia products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary’s AI capabilities,” the Republican chairs of House committees focused on foreign affairs, intelligence, and China said in a joint statement. Rep. Brian Mast, the chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has also demanded that the Department of Commerce share extensive data regarding its investigation into chip smuggling, including by Megaspeed and its affiliates. The Senate Banking Committee will also question Huang in a public hearing on December 3. “Mr. Huang, Nvidia executives, and the company’s board still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with U.S. export controls,” Senator Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democratic member on the committee, said in a statement. “The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what ‘input’ was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement.” When you purchase through links in our articles,

stories.summary: Amazon and Meta are discussing a potential deal that would end a two-month-long blockade of Muse.

sources.name: TechCrunch AI
sources.title: Amazon and Meta reportedly in talks to lift blockade on AI agent Muse
sources.text: Amazon may be having a change of heart about Meta’s AI agent, Muse. The two tech giants are reportedly discussing a potential deal that would allow Meta’s popular AI agent to connect directly to Amazon’s store. The talks would mark a significant reversal from just two months ago, when Muse users discovered they were unable to purchase products on Amazon and instead received an error message when attempting to check out. According to a Wednesday report by Fortune , citing people familiar with the discussions, Amazon and Meta have held multiple rounds of talks about the matter. Two key issues remain under negotiation: how search results would be presented and how advertising would be handled under a potential agreement. One of Amazon’s biggest concerns is how third-party shopping agents like Muse could affect its advertising business. In October, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy argued that few customers were making purchases through outside shopping agents. Amazon may also have been waiting for Muse to mature before agreeing to integrate it with its marketplace. If Muse places the wrong order or creates a problem with a purchase, Amazon could ultimately be left dealing with frustrated customers and unhappy sellers. Fortune reported that executives are concerned that third-party shopping agents could weaken Amazon’s direct relationship with consumers, according to people familiar with the matter. Any potential agreement between Amazon and Meta would reportedly require approval from both companies’ CEOs, Fortune also reported. Meta and Amazon have not yet responded to TechCrunch’s requests for comment. sources.title: Amazon is reportedly in talks to end Muse AI shopping block
sources.text: Amazon is concerned that Muse AI could have an impact on its advertising revenue, according to Fortune. Amazon is concerned that Muse AI could have an impact on its advertising revenue, according to Fortune. Amazon has held talks about letting Meta’s Muse AI agent shop on its online marketplace, according to a report from Fortune . The discussions, which could end Amazon’s block on Muse , reportedly center on the kinds of products the AI agent recommends and the potential impact on the ecommerce giant’s advertising revenue. As reported by Fortune , Amazon is concerned that it could lose advertising revenue by allowing Muse on its site, since it depends on actual humans seeing ads across its online marketplace. It’s also reportedly worried about the quality of the product search results that Muse will present to users, as well as whether the AI agent will affect Amazon’s relationship with customers. Neither Amazon nor Meta immediately responded to The Verge ’s request for comment. Though some online retailers, such as Walmart, Best Buy, Gap, and Sephora, have opened their digital doors to AI agents like Muse, Amazon has been more hesitant. Amazon also blocked Perplexity’s AI agent from shopping on its site, and has instead focused on promoting its own Alexa for Shopping assistant , which customers can now text to shop on their behalf .

stories.title: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’
stories.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei pushes back against rivals’ accusations that he favors surrendering human agency to AI, even as leading AI companies increasingly automate their own research and model development.

sources.name: TechCrunch AI
sources.title: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’
sources.text: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems. In a long X post on Wednesday, Amodei called the suggestion “absurd.” “We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he wrote. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea…No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different.” The statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly. Earlier this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he wanted to ensure people continue to have “agency over the future.” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang also wrote in an essay on X that we “should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.” “It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” Wang wrote. “Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment, and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully.” But in published essays, Amodei claims he has repeatedly advocated for democratic oversight of AI, saying the technology should strengthen democratic institutions and that humans should retain ultimate decision-making power. Amodei noted that there’s a difference between surrendering human free will broadly and the idea that “as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way.” As examples, he gave AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing end-to-end software. Amodei suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement (RSI), or AI that can improve itself without human assistance. Many safety experts see RSI as inevitably leading to a loss of human control, a point Amodei implicitly acknowledged, writing, “we may want limits on this process.” Still, Anthropic is laying the groundwork for RSI by incorporating AI into an increasing share of its own research and development. The company said in June that Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s codebase. An independent assessment published this month by AI safety research nonprofit METR found that Anthropic’s models are improving at about twice their historical rate, primarily driven by AI-assisted research. In its own IPO filings, Anthropic describes how each successive generation of Claude accelerates the development of the next, a process it refers to as “closing the loop.” “As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding,” Amodei wrote. The problem with “meaningful human supervision or understanding” is that AI is already advancing faster than engineers and safety experts can fully audit it, leaving them increasingly reliant on other AI systems to act as judge and jury. The issue compounds when AI models engage in deceptive behavior, particularly when they recognize they’re being evaluated, making them harder to trust and control. Still, Anthropic is by no means the only company that is pursuing RSI or building AI systems to automate more and more human tasks. This week, OpenAI claimed to have solved one of the biggest open problems in computer science — the exact speed limit of matrix multiplication, which is the mathematical engine behind modern computing, including deep learning and physics simulations. In his post, Amodei accused competitors of engaging in a “vibes-based commercial and political positioning,” disingenuously throwing around phrases like “human control and agency” or “AI should just be a tool” without approaching the AI race any differently. “Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation,” Amodei wrote. “Every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . Her work has also appeared in Forbes, Bloomberg, The Atlantic, The Daily Beast, and other publications. sources.title: Dario Amodei (43 años), CEO de Anthropic, rompe su silencio: "No vamos a entregar el control de la humanidad a la IA"
sources.text: Elígenos como tu fuente preferida en Google. Dario Amodei, CEO de Anthropic, defiende que los humanos deben mantener el control sobre la inteligencia artificial y rechaza ceder el libre albedrío a las máquinas. Dario Amodei, responsable de Anthropic, ha compartido en su perfil personal de X sus impresiones acerca del control de la inteligencia artificial y su autonomía , teniendo en cuenta que no cree que se deba "entregar el libre albedrío humano" a los sistemas de inteligencia artificial y que "es absurdo sugerir lo contrario". Esta publicación llega después de que varios líderes tecnológicos de firmas competidoras de Anthropic sugirieran que la compañía estaría participando en el fin del poder de las personas sobre las máquinas y la tecnología. "Jamás deberíamos sacrificar la legitimidad o la autodeterminación en aras de la eficiencia o la seguridad", h a explicado el director ejecutivo de Anthropic en esta publicación , que se extiende más de lo habitual y casi llega a los 7 millones de visualizaciones. Amodei ha hecho su reflexión en X compartiendo, a su vez, una publicación de Axios , que lleva por título: "Los líderes de la discrepan sobre la renuncia al libre albedrío humano", publicada también este mismo miércoles. En este reportaje se indica que "los principales ejecutivos de IA están rechazando cada vez más una visión común dentro de Anthropic: que la humanidad debería renunciar a algún poder de toma de decisiones a los sistemas de inteligencia artificial superinteligentes". Madison Mills, redactora del artículo, sostiene que, aunque los críticos "aún no han llamado a la compañía por su nombre, sus defensas públicas de la agencia y el control humanos apuntan directamente a lo que algunos han llegado a considerar la visión del mundo" de Amodei. En este sentido, Mills recuerda que éste ha afirmado "en repetidas ocasiones" que, cuando los sistemas de IA superen con creces a la inteligencia humana, será preferible delegar la toma de decisiones en casos "críticos para la vida" a la IA y también ha dicho que esta tecnología debería tener la capacidad de supervisar tareas de investigación. Incluso, "distribuir los recursos económicos". Asimismo, recuerda que, dentro de la compañía que desarrolla Claude, "se ha alcanzado el consenso entre algunos empleados en el sentido de que la humanidad cederá de forma segura a la autoridad de los sistemas superinteligentes". Teniendo en cuenta estas acusaciones, el CEO de Anthropic ha asegurado que no está de acuerdo con ésto y que no cree que se le deba "entregar el libre albedrío humano" a los sistemas de inteligencia artificial. "Es absurdo sugerir lo contrario". "He escrito cientos de páginas de ensayos y un tema recurrente en ellos es la necesidad de que la IA se rija por procesos democráticos legítimos", ha insistido Amodei en este texto, que ya reúne más de 18.000 me gusta . Para defender su posición con respecto a la IA, Amodei ha querido aclarar que no apuesta a que esta tecnología tendrá una mayor capacidad que los humanos, sino que, "a medida que los sistemas avanzan, se vuelven capaces de realizar tareas específicas". Con ello, ha defendido que "la IA realice tareas más completas o de mayor envergadura es económicamente valioso y puede impulsar avances importantes en software, medicina, transporte, energía, etc." . "Es claramente deseable en muchos casos y salvará muchas vidas", ha añadido. Con ello, ha sostenido que, aunque Claude esté experimentando un gran avance en sus tareas, no creen que sea seguro que esta IA "construya sucesivos modelos de vanguardia de forma totalmente autónoma, sin una supervisión o comprensión humana significativa". Finalmente, ha señalado a los que le habrían atribuido unas opiniones que realmente no tiene, asegurando qu e "algunos directores ejecutivos de empresas de IA están adoptando una especie de posicionamiento comercial y político basado en las sensaciones". "Repiten eslóganes como control y autonomía humanos o la IA debería ser solo una herramienta, sin hacer realmente nada diferente en sus productos ni tomarse en serio las difíciles cuestiones que subyacen a estos eslóganes", ha rematado.

recent_posts.summary: O Google reescreveu o aplicativo para rodar em aparelhos com pouca memória da linha Android Go, levando o assistente de IA a mais usuários.

recent_posts.title: Nvidia lança minidesktops RTX Spark para rodar IA local
recent_posts.summary: Computadores compactos da Asus, da Dell e da MSI usam a plataforma RTX Spark para rodar agentes, gerar imagem e vídeo e ajustar modelos sem depender da nuvem, segundo a Nvidia.

recent_posts.title: OpenAI usa seus modelos de IA para melhorar projeto de chips com a AMD
recent_posts.summary: A empresa diz ter reduzido área de circuitos do seu chip Jalapeño e, em parceria com a AMD, melhorado métricas de desempenho de GPUs e CPUs, segundo comunicado oficial.

recent_posts.title: Anthropic fecha IPO em US$ 119,5 bi com aporte de fabricantes de chip
recent_posts.summary: A empresa confirmou o exercício total da opção dos subscritores e uma colocação privada com AMD, Broadcom, Google, Microsoft, Nvidia e outras, segundo comunicado oficial.

recent_posts.title: Meta leva o Muse, seu agente pessoal de IA, para a Austrália
recent_posts.summary: Com parceiros locais em compras, imóveis e academia, o assistente chega ao terceiro mercado confirmado, segundo a própria empresa.

recent_posts.title: Ações da Anthropic caem no segundo dia e arrastam a Nasdaq
recent_posts.summary: A dona do Claude recuou perto do preço do IPO enquanto chips e bolsas da Ásia e da Europa também caíam, segundo o Guardian e a CNBC.

recent_posts.title: Matemático da Anthropic diz ter resolvido a Hipótese de Riemann
recent_posts.summary: Levent Alpöge publicou a demonstração em seu site pessoal dias após o IPO da Anthropic; a prova ainda não foi verificada de forma independente.

recent_posts.title: Apple contrata engenheiros para criar agente de IA próprio
recent_posts.summary: Vaga removida descrevia um assistente capaz de operar o computador inteiro, segundo a Bloomberg, citada pela TechCrunch e pelo The Verge.

recent_posts.title: Onda de apagões nos EUA reabre debate sobre o papel da IA
recent_posts.summary: Microsoft, FAA, bancos e Apple Pay falharam em dias recentes; autoridades negam ataque, mas especialistas discordam sobre o papel da IA.

recent_posts.title: Sete fundadores da Anthropic embolsam US$ 280 milhões cada no IPO
recent_posts.summary: Documentos da abertura de capital mostram que Amazon e Google também ficam com 28% da empresa, segundo TechCrunch e Fortune.

recent_posts.title: Trump ameaça taxar empresas dos EUA por data centers no exterior
recent_posts.summary: Em coletiva na Casa Branca, presidente disse que vai impedir empresas americanas de erguer data centers em outros países e prometeu um "imposto tremendo" para quem descumprir, segundo a CNBC e o The Verge.

recent_posts.title: Gemini no Mac ganha modo que opera outros programas sozinho
recent_posts.summary: Recurso "Computer Use" chega ao aplicativo de Mac e deixa o assistente do Google clicar, digitar e navegar em nome do usuário, segundo a SiliconANGLE e o Engadget.

recent_posts.title: Google transforma Gemini em assistente que executa tarefas
recent_posts.summary: Novo modo "Tarefas" chega de graça a seis países e usa o modelo Gemini 4 Hydrogen para agendar compromissos, pagar contas e fazer compras, segundo o Google e o TechCrunch.

recent_posts.title: Microsoft e Salesforce lançam integração batizada Copilotforce
recent_posts.summary: Parceria conecta dados e ações do Salesforce ao Copilot, Teams e Fabric da Microsoft, com plugin em teste público e a Accenture como primeira cliente piloto, segundo as duas empresas.

recent_posts.title: Anthropic estreia na Nasdaq e dispara para US$ 2 trilhões
recent_posts.summary: Ações da dona do Claude abriram em alta de 34% sobre o preço do IPO, a maior oferta pública já registrada em valor captado, segundo a CNBC e a Fortune.
